transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Yeah, thanks for fitting me in. So, um, I guess what brings me in is... well, it's work stuff, mostly. I'm an electrician, been in the trade for over two decades, so I know what I'm doing, right? I took some college classes before I got into my apprenticeship, so I know the theory, I know the code inside and out. But lately—well, I say lately, it's been getting a lot worse recently—I just keep going back over my jobs again and again. 

It's honestly exhausting. Like, I'll finish up a panel, a really basic install that I could do in my sleep, and I'll just stand there checking the breakers. I have to touch them, make sure they're seated right. Then I check the labels, read them over and over to make sure I didn't misspell a word or write down the wrong circuit number. I even check my torque marks on the lugs—you know, the little marker lines we draw to show a screw is tightened down to spec? I'll just stare at them. I've even started taking photos of the panels with my phone before I put the cover on, just so I can zoom in on the picture when I'm in my truck to reassure myself. 

But even that isn't enough sometimes! Just last Tuesday, I was halfway home, sitting in rush hour traffic on the interstate, and I started thinking about this one ground wire, and I actually turned my truck around and drove all the way back to the job site. Just to look at it. And of course, it was fine. It's getting to the point where a simple install takes way, way longer than it should. It's eating up my whole day. And, you know, construction runs on a tight schedule, so people are starting to notice. My foreman asked me what was taking so long on a basic subpanel the other day, and I didn't know what to tell him, because I can't exactly say I spent forty-five minutes just re-reading the breaker labels and wiggling wires. I just... I can't seem to stop myself from doing it.
Do you feel anxious or upset when you're not able to check your work as many times as you want?

Oh man, anxious doesn't even begin to cover it. It's... it's like this physical knot right here in my chest, just pulling tight. If I have to leave a site—say the general contractor is locking up the building for the day and yelling at everyone to clear out, so I can't do my usual routine—I am just an absolute wreck. 

Because, well, even after I *know* I checked a panel or a disconnect, you know, I logically know I put my torque wrench on it and did my job like a professional... this thought just keeps barging in on me. It doesn't matter how many times I tell myself I did it right. My brain just goes, 'Hey, what if you missed one loose neutral?' Or maybe I left a stray piece of copper wire in there, or just... something, anything that could arc and start a fire. And being an electrician, you know the stakes, right? A bad connection means resistance, resistance means heat, and heat means a fire in a building where people might be sleeping or working. 

So I'll get in my truck, and I try to shake it off. I really do. I'll crank up the radio, roll the windows down, try to think about what I'm going to grill for dinner, tell myself I've had my journeyman card for twenty years and I don't make rookie mistakes. Just anything to distract myself. But it doesn't work. The thought just follows me all the way home. I'll be sitting at the kitchen table, and my wife will be talking to me about her day, and I'm just staring at my plate, completely consumed by this vivid image of a panel smoking and catching fire all because I couldn't go back and check that one neutral wire one last time. It ruins my whole evening. It's just... it's torture, honestly, not being able to go back and make sure.
Do you have these repetitive checking behaviors in other areas of your life, outside of your work as an electrician?

No, not really. I mean, it's pretty much just the electrical work. Like, at home, I'm fine. I don't go around checking the stove or the locks or anything like that. My wife actually jokes that I'm the opposite of that guy who checks the door handle ten times before leaving the house, because half the time I forget to lock the deadbolt when I come in from the garage. She's always getting on me about it, saying, "You know anyone could just walk right in here, right?" And I'll just shrug and go lock it. It doesn't bother me. 

And, you know, it's funny, because you'd think if my brain was wired to worry about things catching fire, I'd be checking the coffee maker or the dryer lint trap or something, right? But I just... I don't. I make my coffee in the morning, I turn the machine off—or maybe I leave it on, it has an auto-shutoff anyway—and I walk out the door. I don't give it a second thought. Same thing with my truck. I don't check the tires or the oil obsessively. I just get in, turn the key, and go. 

It really is just my job. And I think... well, I've thought about this a lot, sitting in traffic and all... I think it's because when I'm at work, it's *my* name on the line. It's my license, my reputation. If I wire a house and it burns down, that's on me. The guilt of that, the responsibility... it's just so heavy. But at home, if the coffee maker shorts out, well, that's a faulty appliance, you know? It's not because I didn't torque a lug down to the exact inch-pound. So yeah, it's really just the job site where I get stuck in these loops. The rest of my life is pretty normal, honestly. Well, as normal as it can be when you're exhausted all the time from stressing about work.
Do you feel like these thoughts about checking your electrical work are a part of you, or do they feel like they're coming from outside of yourself?

Outside of myself? Um... I'm not sure I follow exactly what you mean by that. Like, if you mean am I hearing voices or something, like someone else is putting the thoughts in my head? No, no, nothing like that. It's definitely me. It's my own voice in my head, you know? But... well, I guess it feels like a part of me that just won't listen to reason. It's like my brain—my own brain—is just getting stuck in a rut and spinning its tires. 

I'll be driving, right, and it's my own thought popping up saying, 'Hey, did you really tighten that lug on phase B?' And I'll answer myself, in my head, 'Yes, I tightened it, I saw the marker line.' But then that same part of my brain just pushes back and goes, 'Are you sure? Because if you're wrong, the place burns down.' So it's a hundred percent me, it's just... it's like I'm arguing with myself. And it's exhausting, honestly, because you can't walk away from an argument when it's happening inside your own skull. 

I've always been a careful guy, you know? Even back when I was taking those college classes before my apprenticeship, I was the guy double-checking my math on the exams before I handed them in. So being careful, wanting to do things right, that is definitely a part of who I am. I take pride in it. But this... this is like that careful part of me drank ten pots of coffee and just completely took over the steering wheel. It's me, but it's me turned up to a level that I don't want to be at. I don't want to be doing it. I know it's my own worry, but I just can't seem to turn the volume down on it, no matter how much I try to logic my way out of it. So yeah, it's me. It's just a really, really frustrating version of me that won't quit.
Are these thoughts and behaviors affecting your relationships with family and friends outside of work?

Well, yeah, they really are. I mean, it bleeds over into everything, honestly, even though I try so hard to keep it contained to the job site. Because, see, the thing is, my whole business schedule is just... it is slipping, badly. It is getting completely thrown out of whack. Jobs that I should absolutely be able to finish in one single visit, you know, standard stuff I have done a thousand times, they end up turning into these endless callbacks and extra checks. And I am the one initiating them! I will make up an excuse to the general contractor about needing to verify a circuit just to get back in the building. And I can tell it is starting to cost me client confidence. They look at me sideways, wondering why the experienced guy is coming back to a finished job. And it is eating into my time with the apprentices, too, which really bothers me. Instead of teaching them the trade, I am leaving them sitting in the van while I go back inside for the third time to stare at a panel.

And because of all that, or just because my head is stuck in that loop... it definitely hits my personal life, like you were asking. I have been skipping out on things I used to really enjoy doing after work. My buddy has a bowling league on Thursday nights, and my wife and I used to do dinners with the neighbors, but lately, I just... I can't do it. I will get home, and I am just so tied up mentally reviewing a job, sitting in my recliner just agonizing over whether I need to drive all the way back across town to the site to check my work. I end up just staying home, completely distracted. So, yeah, I am missing out on a lot, and my friends and my wife, they are definitely getting the short end of the stick because even when I am home, I am just never fully there anymore. I am always just worrying about whether I need to go back.
Do you feel like these obsessive thoughts about your electrical work are in line with your own values and beliefs?

Well, yes and no, I guess. Mostly no. I mean, like I was saying earlier, I definitely value doing a good, safe job. The National Electrical Code exists for a reason, you know? You don't mess around with electricity. So in that sense, wanting things to be safe is a huge part of my belief system. I'm a professional. 

But these specific thoughts? The way they act? No, that doesn't feel like it lines up with who I want to be at all. It feels more like a... like a hijacking, honestly. Because, see, even after I know I checked a panel or a disconnect—like, I can literally picture myself standing there, I know I put the torque screwdriver on the lugs, I know I did the pull test on the wires—this thought just keeps barging in on me. It doesn't care about my values or what I know is true. It just forces its way in, whispering that maybe I missed one loose neutral. And a loose neutral, doc, that's bad news. That's how things heat up, that's how you get arcing, and before you know it, you've left something that could start a fire. 

And I don't *want* to be thinking about that. It's not like I sit down and decide to review my day. I try to shake it off, I really do. I'll get in the truck, I'll crank up the classic rock station, or I'll try to call my wife to ask what we're doing for dinner, just anything to drown it out. But it just follows me all the way home. It's like it's sitting right there in the passenger seat with me, tapping me on the shoulder the whole drive. 

So if you're asking if this fits with how I want to live my life, absolutely not. My values are about doing a solid day's work, packing up my tools, and going home to be a normal husband and a normal guy. But these thoughts just don't respect that boundary. They just barge right over it and ruin the whole evening, no matter how hard I try to push them away. It's just... it's not me choosing to do this, if that makes sense.
How would you rate the distress these thoughts cause you, on a scale from 1 to 10?

Oh, a number... man, I guess on a scale of one to ten, I'd probably have to put it at a... maybe a solid seven? Sometimes an eight, depending on the day and the specific job. 

Because, like I was just saying a minute ago about that whole loose neutral thing... it's the sheer exhaustion of it that really drives that number up. The distress isn't just a quick little worry, it's this heavy, sinking feeling in my gut. I mean, I *know* I checked that panel. I know I checked the disconnect. I can literally see my hands doing the work in my memory. But then that thought just barges right back in, completely uninvited, telling me I definitely left something that's gonna spark and start a fire. 

And the distress comes from the fact that I just can't get rid of it. I try to shake it off, I really do try everything I can think of, but it just latches onto me and follows me all the way home, every single mile of the commute. By the time I pull into my driveway, my stomach is in absolute knots, and my jaw aches from clenching it the whole drive. You know, you'd think after all my years in the trade, I'd be able to just leave the job at the job site, but it just rides shotgun with me and refuses to let me relax. So yeah, I'd say a seven or an eight, easy, because fighting that feeling day in and day out just drains everything out of me.
Are you finding it difficult to meet your responsibilities at work or at home because of these thoughts and behaviors?

Yeah, I mean, I know I touched on this a little bit earlier when we first started talking, but honestly, yes, it's making it incredibly hard to keep up with everything. It's just a huge mess, to be perfectly frank with you. 

At work, my business schedule is just completely slipping away from me. It's embarrassing, really. I've been doing this for years, and these jobs... you know, jobs that I should absolutely be able to knock out in one single, straightforward visit, they're turning into these ridiculous callbacks. And the worst part is, it's not because the client called me with a problem! It's because *I'm* the one doing all these extra checks. I'll pack up all my tools, get the van loaded, drive halfway down the road, and then my brain just won't let it go, so I turn right back around. And the general contractors, they definitely notice. You can't hide that kind of thing on a busy job site. It is absolutely starting to cost me client confidence. They're looking at me sideways, probably thinking, 'Why is this veteran guy coming back to stare at a panel he finished three hours ago?' 

And my apprentices... man, that's what really gets me when it comes to my responsibilities. I have a duty to teach these young guys the trade, you know? Show them the ropes. And instead, I'm leaving them just sitting there idling in the van while I go back inside for the third time to double-check my own work. It's not fair to them, and it makes me feel like a terrible boss.

And then at home... yeah, my responsibilities there are taking a huge hit, too. Like I mentioned about skipping out on the bowling league and the dinners with the neighbors... it's because I'm just not *present* anymore. I'm skipping all these things I used to really enjoy after work because my brain is still on the clock. Even when I'm physically sitting in my own living room, I'm completely tied up mentally reviewing a job. My wife will be trying to talk to me, or maybe there's stuff around the house that needs doing, and I'm just sitting there in my recliner, totally zoned out, agonizing over whether I need to get back in the truck and drive all the way across town to check a circuit. So I'm just skipping out on my actual life, basically. I'm not being the boss I need to be, and I'm not being the husband I need to be, because all my energy is just getting eaten alive by worrying about whether I need to go back to the site.
Are there any situations or activities where you feel like you can temporarily escape or distract yourself from these obsessive thoughts about your electrical work?

Man, I wish I could give you a nice, easy list of things that work, I really do. But honestly? Not really. I mean, I try... I try so hard to just find a little peace and quiet in my own head. Like, I used to love just going out to the garage on a weekend and tinkering with my old Chevy, or just sitting down to watch a football game with a cold beer. You'd think that would be enough to distract a guy, right? Just completely check out for a couple of hours and forget about the job. 

But it just doesn't happen like that anymore. It always comes back to exactly what I was telling you earlier. I'll be right in the middle of something supposedly relaxing, and even after I *know*—like, for an absolute fact, with my own two eyes—that I checked a panel or a disconnect, this thought just keeps barging right in on me. It doesn't matter if I'm miles away from a job site or if it's a Sunday afternoon. I'll be sitting there holding a wrench or watching a play on TV, and suddenly my brain is just screaming that maybe I missed one loose neutral. That maybe I left something behind that could start a fire. 

And once that thought is there, the distraction is just... well, it's totally ruined. I try to shake it off, you know, I'll turn the TV up louder or try to focus really, really hard on whatever I'm doing with my hands, but it just doesn't work. Like I said, it just follows me all the way home from the site, and then it just stays with me, following me into every single corner of my house. There's just no real escape from it, no matter how hard I try to force myself to focus on something else. It just won't let me be.
Are these obsessive thoughts and behaviors causing significant problems in your relationships with your wife and friends, beyond just missing social events?

Well, yeah... I mean, I know I'm probably sounding like a broken record here, bringing it right back to what I was just telling you, but it all just bleeds together, you know? It really does. With my wife... it's definitely causing some real friction. It's way beyond just missing the neighborhood dinners or the bowling league. It's the fact that I'm physically sitting right there in the room with her, but my mind is a million miles away. She'll be telling me about her day, or trying to talk about, I don't know, fixing the gutters or something, and I'm just sitting there staring a hole in the wall because I am completely tied up mentally reviewing a job I finished six hours ago. I'm sitting there agonizing, literally sweating sometimes, worrying about whether I need to get my boots back on and drive all the way back to the site. 

And she sees that. She's not blind, she knows I'm not listening to a word she's saying. It makes her feel like she doesn't matter, which just kills me, but I can't snap out of it. And a lot of that tension comes from the work stuff I mentioned... the fact that my business schedule is slipping so badly. That stress doesn't just stay in the work van. When I'm turning jobs that should absolutely be one single, easy visit into these ridiculous callbacks and extra checks, I'm losing time, and I'm bringing all that frustration straight into my living room. 

I'll be sitting at the dinner table, but in my head, I'm chewing on how this is starting to cost me client confidence, and how I'm wasting valuable time with the apprentices who are relying on me to actually teach them the trade instead of watching me double-check a breaker for the fourth time. That kind of guilt really weighs on a guy. It eats at you. So when my friends call up and want to grab a beer or do something on a Saturday, I just... I blow them off. I've been skipping all those things I used to really enjoy after work because my brain just absolutely refuses to clock out. So yeah, my buddies probably think I'm just being a jerk and icing them out, and my wife is just exhausted from trying to pull me out of my own head every single night. It's putting a huge strain on everybody.

Have you noticed these obsessive thoughts about your electrical work and the need to check things repeatedly following you consistently every day, or are there days when you can manage to distract yourself from them for longer periods?

Every single day. I mean, I really wish I could sit here and tell you that, you know, maybe on a Wednesday or a Thursday I get a break and I can just pack up my tools, turn the key in the ignition, and drive away like a normal guy. But... no, it's every day. There aren't any periods where I can just turn it off or distract myself for longer stretches. 

Like I was trying to explain a minute ago, it's just this constant, exhausting loop. I can be standing right there on the site, and even after I *know*—and I mean absolutely know for a fact because I just stared right at it and put my own hands on it—that I checked a panel or a disconnect, this... this thought just keeps barging right in on me anyway. It's like my brain completely overrides my own eyes. It just starts nagging at me, telling me that maybe, just maybe, I missed one loose neutral somewhere in that box. Or maybe I stripped a wire a little too far and left something that could spark and start a fire. 

And a fire... I mean, you have to understand, in my line of work, that's people's lives, their homes, their families, you know? That's a heavy, heavy thing to carry around in your head. So I try to shake it off. I really do try. I'll get in the work van, roll down the windows to let the air hit my face, crank up the radio to some classic rock, just try to force myself to think about literally anything else... but it doesn't matter. It just follows me all the way home. Every single day, on every single job. It rides shotgun with me all the way back to my driveway, and there's just no shaking it, no matter what day of the week it is. I never get a day off from it.
Are you finding that these obsessive thoughts and behaviors are significantly interfering with your ability to function in your daily life, beyond just the issues at work?

Yeah, I mean, like I was kind of getting at earlier... it's just bleeding into absolutely everything. It’s not just a bad day on the site, it’s... well, it’s my whole life right now. I know I brought up the business side of things a minute ago, but it really is a huge deal and it messes up my whole day. My entire business schedule is just slipping so badly. I’ve been doing this a long time, and these jobs... I mean, they should be simple. They should absolutely be one single visit—you go in, you do the work, you pack up, and you're done. But I’m turning them into these endless callbacks and all these extra checks because I just can't force myself to walk away. 

And the worst part is, I can see it starting to really cost me client confidence. You can just tell by the way a homeowner looks at you when you show up at their door again to look at a breaker box you already signed off on yesterday. They start wondering if you actually know what you're doing, and that hurts. And then there are my apprentices. These young guys are relying on me, you know? I’m supposed to be passing on a trade, teaching them how to do things right, and instead, I'm losing all this valuable time with them because they're just standing around holding a flashlight while I second-guess myself for the tenth time. 

And then, you know, the clock strikes five, but I’m not really off the clock. That's where the rest of my daily life just completely falls apart. Like I said about my wife and my buddies... I’ve just been skipping everything. All those little things I used to really enjoy after work, I just can't do them anymore. I'll try to sit down and relax, but I’m just totally tied up in my own head, sitting there mentally reviewing every single wire nut and screw from a job I left hours ago. I can't focus on a conversation or a hobby because I'm just sitting there agonizing, worrying myself sick about whether I need to get back in the truck and drive all the way back out there to check it again. It just paralyzes me, doc. It takes up so much space in my head that there's just no room left for anything else.
Are your obsessive thoughts about checking your electrical work more about the fear of missing something or the fear of what could happen if something goes wrong?

Well, it’s... I guess it’s really both, but the fear of what could happen is the engine driving the whole thing, if that makes sense. Like I was telling you a little bit earlier, even after I absolutely *know* I checked a panel or a disconnect—I mean, I can literally remember the feeling of the screwdriver in my hand, I know I torqued the lugs down tight—this thought just keeps barging right in on me anyway. It just crashes right through all my logic and common sense. 

And it always goes straight to the absolute worst-case scenario. It’s not just, 'Oh, I made a sloppy connection and the lights might flicker.' It’s that nagging voice telling me that maybe, just maybe, I missed one loose neutral, or maybe I left a wire stripped just a fraction of an inch too far, and that tiny little oversight is going to arc inside the wall, and then it’s going to start a fire. 

And that’s the part that just completely grips me. The fire. Because, you know, a fire isn't just a simple callback to fix a broken outlet on a Tuesday morning. A fire means the whole house goes up in smoke. It means a family could lose every single thing they own, all their memories, or worse, they could get hurt or... or killed, all because I was the last guy standing there with my hands in that breaker box. That consequence is just so massive, so terrifying, that it makes the fear of missing something completely unbearable. It magnifies it a thousand times over. 

So I try to shake it off, I really do try. Like I was saying before, I'll get in the van, turn the radio up loud, roll the windows down, try to convince myself I’m being ridiculous because I *know* I checked it. I looked right at it. But the thought of that house burning down... it just doesn't care about my logic. It follows me all the way home. It sits there in the passenger seat with me at every single stoplight, follows me up the driveway, and walks right through the front door with me. It’s just this endless cycle over that one tiny mistake turning into a total disaster, and I just can't shut it off, no matter how hard I try to reason with myself.
Are these obsessive thoughts and behaviors significantly impacting your overall quality of life?

Yeah, doc, absolutely. I know I keep circling back to this, and I feel like I'm beating a dead horse here, but it really is ruining my quality of life. Like I was saying a few minutes ago about the business side of things... my schedule is just slipping so far behind because of this. Jobs that I should absolutely be finishing in one single visit—like, bread and butter stuff I've done a thousand times—they just keep turning into these endless callbacks and extra checks. 

And the toll it takes on my reputation... I mean, I mentioned it's costing me client confidence, but it's more than just losing a referral. It's honestly humiliating. You see the look on a homeowner's face when you pull up to their house for the second or third time to look at a subpanel you already told them was perfectly fine. They start looking at you like you're a hack, like maybe they hired the wrong guy, and I've spent twenty years building this business, you know? And the apprentices, like I brought up earlier, I'm losing all that valuable time with them. They're just standing around watching me second-guess myself instead of actually learning the trade. It makes me feel like I'm failing them as a mentor.

And then, my personal life... well, like I told you, I'm just skipping all the things I used to actually enjoy after work. I used to love just going out to the garage and tinkering with my old truck, or just sitting down with my wife to watch a movie and actually relaxing. But now? I can't even sit through a half-hour TV show. I'm physically sitting there on the couch, but mentally, I'm miles away, just completely tied up reviewing every single step of a job I left hours ago. I just sit there stewing, worrying myself sick about whether I need to grab my keys, get back in the van, and drive all the way back out there in the dark just to check a connection one more time. It just drains the life out of you. There's no joy in anything right now because I'm never really off the clock in my head. Everything else just takes a back seat to the worry.
Do you feel like checking your work repeatedly is something you do to maintain control over the situation, or is it primarily driven by the fear of something going wrong?

Well, like I was saying about the fire, it’s definitely the fear that’s driving it, but... but I guess because I'm so terrified of that worst-case scenario, I try to get control over it by doing all this checking. And honestly, that's really the whole reason I'm sitting here talking to you today. What brings me in is that I just keep going back over jobs again and again, and it's getting completely out of hand. 

I mean, I'm not just giving a panel a quick once-over before I screw the cover on like a normal guy would. I'm checking the breakers, physically pushing on them to make sure they're seated. I'm checking the labels I wrote out, double-checking the torque marks on every single lug to make absolutely sure I tightened them to spec. I've even started taking photos... like, I have a whole album on my phone that's just pictures of the inside of breaker boxes. I'll take a picture of the neutral bar, the ground bar, the main lugs, just so I can zoom in on the connections when I get home. 

But even that doesn't always work, you know? Because I'll be looking at the picture at a stoplight or sitting on my couch, and I'll think, "Wait, is that a shadow, or did I leave a strand of copper sticking out?" And then... then I end up actually driving back to a site sometimes. I'll literally turn the van around in rush hour traffic, or get up from the dinner table, just to go look at it with my own eyes again to prove to myself it's fine. Because of all this, a simple install—something I could have done blindfolded ten years ago—it just takes way, way longer than it should. And people are really starting to notice. The homeowners are noticing how long I'm down in the basement, my apprentices are noticing that I'm taking pictures of wires... it's just exhausting trying to control that fear by checking everything a hundred times.
Do you feel like checking your work repeatedly is more about preventing something bad from happening or about feeling in control of the situation?

Well, yeah, like I was just saying a second ago, doc, it’s definitely about preventing that bad thing from happening. The fire, the disaster, all of that. I mean, I don't really feel like I'm in control of the situation at all, to be honest with you. If I had any actual control, I wouldn't be doing all this, you know? 

Because, like I mentioned, what really brings me in here to see you today is the fact that I just keep going back over these jobs again and again, and I literally cannot stop myself. I know I just ran through the whole list with you—checking the breakers, making sure the labels are perfectly accurate, double and triple-checking the torque marks on the lugs, taking all those photos on my phone—but I do all of that because I'm just so terrified of what happens if I don't. I'm trying to prevent a tragedy, not feel like the boss of the breaker box. 

And like I said, even with all those checks, I'll still end up driving back to a site sometimes. I'll just completely turn the van around in the middle of traffic. And it's just... it's ruining everything. A perfectly simple install, something that should be a quick in-and-out job for a guy with my experience, it just takes way, way longer than it ever should because I'm stuck in this endless loop of trying to prevent a disaster. And like I said before, people are really starting to notice. You just can't hide it when you're taking three times as long on a basic panel swap. The apprentices see me doing it, the clients see me doing it... so no, I don't feel in control at all. I just feel like I'm constantly trying to outrun a catastrophe, and it's exhausting.
Is your need to repeatedly check your work more about ensuring everything is perfect or about avoiding something going wrong?

Yeah, doc, I feel like we're kind of beating the same drum here, but to answer your question—no, it's really not about perfection at all. I don't care if a wire isn't bent at a perfect ninety-degree angle, or if the panel looks perfectly symmetrical, you know? I've been in the trade long enough to know that perfect doesn't exist in an old house. It's absolutely about avoiding a disaster. It's exactly like I was just saying... it's the fire. It's always the fire. 

Let me try to explain how it actually feels in my head, because it's... well, it's hard to describe unless you're living it. It's like... even after I know, for a fact, that I checked a panel or a disconnect—like, I physically know I just stood there and looked at it, tightened everything, put the cover back on—this thought just keeps barging in on me. It just kicks the door down in my brain out of nowhere and says, "Hey, wait a minute, maybe you missed one loose neutral. Maybe you left something in there that's gonna arc and start a fire tonight." 

And I really, really try to shake it off.
